{{Short description|Attempt to demonstrate the 4th dimension in visual arts}}
[[File:Jouffret.gif|thumb|An illustration from Jouffret's ''Traité élémentaire de géométrie à quatre dimensions''. The book, which influenced Picasso, was given to him by Princet.]]
New possibilities opened up by the concept of [[four-dimensional space]] (and difficulties involved in trying to visualize it) helped inspire many modern artists in the first half of the twentieth century. Early [[Cubists]], [[Surrealists]], [[Futurists]], and [[Abstract art|abstract]] artists took ideas from [[Higher-dimensional space|higher-dimensional]] mathematics and used them to radically advance their work.{{sfnp|Henderson|2013}}

== Early influence ==
{{further|Proto-Cubism|Mathematics and art}}
[[File:Picasso Portrait of Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler 1910.jpg|thumb|[[Pablo Picasso]], 1910 ''Portrait of [[Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler]]'', [[Art Institute of Chicago]]]]
[[File:Jean Metzinger, 1910, Nu à la cheminée, published in Les Peintres Cubistes, 1913.jpg|thumb|[[Jean Metzinger]], 1910, ''[[Nu à la cheminée]] (Nude)''. Exhibited at the 1910 Salon d'Automne. Black and white scan from ''[[The Cubist Painters, Aesthetic Meditations|Les Peintres Cubistes]]'' by Guillaume Apollinaire, 1913. Dimensions and whereabouts unknown.]]
[[File:Albert Gleizes, 1913, Portrait de l’éditeur Eugène Figuière (The Publisher Eugene Figuiere), oil on canvas, 143.5 x 101.5 cm, Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon.jpg|thumb|[[Albert Gleizes]], 1913, ''[[Portrait de l’éditeur Eugène Figuière (Gleizes)|Portrait de l’éditeur Eugène Figuière (The Publisher Eugene Figuiere)]]'', [[Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon]]]]

French [[mathematician]] [[Maurice Princet]] was known as "le mathématicien du cubisme" ("the mathematician of cubism").<ref>{{cite book |last=Décimo |first=Marc |title=Maurice Princet, Le Mathématicien du Cubisme |year=2007 |publisher=Éditions L'Echoppe |location=Paris |language=fr |isbn=978-2-84068-191-5}}</ref> An associate of the [[School of Paris]]—a group of [[Avant-garde|avant-gardists]] including [[Pablo Picasso]], [[Guillaume Apollinaire]], [[Max Jacob]], [[Jean Metzinger]], and [[Marcel Duchamp]]—Princet is credited with introducing the work of [[Henri Poincaré]] and the concept of the "[[Four-dimensional space|fourth dimension]]" to the cubists at the [[Le Bateau-Lavoir|Bateau-Lavoir]] during the first decade of the 20th century.<ref name="Miller">{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Arthur I. |title=Einstein, Picasso: space, time, and beauty that causes havoc |location=New York |publisher=Basic Books |year=2001 |type=Print |page=[https://archive.org/details/einsteinpicassos00mill/page/101 101] |isbn=0-465-01859-9 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/einsteinpicassos00mill/page/101 }}</ref>

Princet introduced Picasso to [[Esprit Jouffret]]'s ''Traité élémentaire de géométrie à quatre dimensions'' (''Elementary Treatise on the Geometry of Four Dimensions'', 1903),<ref>{{cite book |last=Jouffret |first=Esprit |title=Traité élémentaire de géométrie à quatre dimensions et introduction à la géométrie à n dimensions |url=https://historical.library.cornell.edu/cgi-bin/cul.math/docviewer?did=04810001 |access-date=2008-02-06 |year=1903 |publisher=Gauthier-Villars |location=Paris |language=fr |oclc=1445172}}</ref> a popularization of Poincaré's ''Science and Hypothesis'' in which Jouffret described [[hypercube]]s and other complex [[Polyhedron|polyhedra]] in four [[dimension]]s and projected them onto the two-dimensional page. Picasso's ''[[Portrait of Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler]]'' in 1910 was an important work for the artist, who spent many months shaping it.<ref>{{cite book |last=Robbin |first=Tony |title=Shadows of Reality: The Fourth Dimension in Relativity, Cubism, and Modern Thought |page=28 |location=New Haven |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |type=Print |year=2006|isbn= 978-0-300-11039-5}}</ref> The portrait bears similarities to Jouffret's work and shows a distinct movement away from the [[Proto-Cubism|Proto-Cubist]] [[fauvism]] displayed in ''[[Les Demoiselles d'Avignon]]'', to a more considered analysis of space and form.<ref>{{cite book |last=Robbin |first=Tony |title=Shadows of Reality: The Fourth Dimension in Relativity, Cubism, and Modern Thought  |location=New Haven |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |type=Print|pages=28–30 |year=2006|isbn= 978-0-300-11039-5}}</ref>

Early cubist [[Max Weber (artist)|Max Weber]] wrote an article entitled "In The Fourth Dimension from a Plastic Point of View", for [[Alfred Stieglitz]]'s July 1910 issue of ''[[Camera Work]]''. In the piece, Weber states,<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Max |last1=Weber |author-link=Max Weber |year=1910 |title=In The Fourth Dimension from a Plastic Point of View |journal= [[Camera Work]]|volume= 31|issue= July 1910}}</ref> "In plastic art, I believe, there is a fourth dimension which may be described as the consciousness of a great and overwhelming sense of space-magnitude in all directions at one time, and is brought into existence through the three known measurements."

Another influence on the School of Paris was that of [[Jean Metzinger]] and [[Albert Gleizes]], both painters and theoreticians. The first major treatise written on the subject of Cubism was their 1912 collaboration ''[[Du "Cubisme"]]'', which says that:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gleizes |first1=Albert |last2=Metzinger |first2=Jean |title=Du Cubisme [translated from French] |date=1913 |publisher=T.F. Unwin |location=London}}</ref><blockquote> "If we wished to relate the space of the [Cubist] painters to geometry, we should have to refer it to the non-Euclidian mathematicians; we should have to study, at some length, certain of [[Bernhard Riemann#Riemannian geometry|Riemann's theorems]]."</blockquote>

The American modernist painter and photographer [[Morton Livingston Schamberg]] wrote in 1910 two letters to [[Walter Pach]],<ref>Letter from Schamberg in Philadelphia to Walter Pach in Paris, 29 December 1910, Pach Papers, Reel: 4216, fr. 856</ref><ref>Letter from Schamberg in Philadelphia to Pach in Paris, 29
December 1910, fr. 857</ref> parts of which were published in a review of the [[Armory Show|1913 Armory Show]] for ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'',<ref>Morton Livingston Schamberg, "Post-Impression Exhibit Awaited", ''The Philadelphia Inquirer'', 19 January 1913, col. 2, p. 3</ref> about the influence of the fourth dimension on avant-garde painting; describing how the artists' employed "harmonic use of forms" distinguishing between the "representation or rendering of space and the designing in space":<ref>{{cite book |last1=Oja|first1=Carol J.|title=Making Music Modern: New York in the 1920s|page=84|date=February 2000|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]], USA}}{{ISBN|9780195162578}}</ref><ref>[https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/handle/2152/33294 Jill Anderson Kyle, ''Cézanne and American Painting 1900 to 1920''], The University of Texas at Austin, 1995</ref><blockquote>If we still further add to design in the third dimension, a consideration of weight, pressure, resistance, movement, as distinguished from motion, we arrive at what may legitimately be called design in the fourth dimension, or the harmonic use of what may arbitrarily be called volume. It is only at this point that we can appreciate the masterly productions of such a man as Cézanne.</blockquote>

Cézanne's explorations of geometric simplification and optical phenomena inspired the Cubists to experiment with [[Simultaneity (art)|simultaneity]], complex multiple views of the same subject, as observed from differing viewpoints at the same time.<ref>Christopher Green, ''Cubism, Meanings and interpretations'', MoMA, Grove Art Online, Oxford University Press, 2009</ref>

== Dimensionist manifesto ==
In 1936 in Paris, [[Charles Sirato|Charles Tamkó Sirató]] published his ''Manifeste Dimensioniste'',<ref name="dimensionalist">{{cite web |url=http://artpool.hu/TamkoSirato/manifest.html |title=Dimensionist Manifesto |first1=Charles Tamkó |last1=Sirató |location=Paris |year=1936 |format=[[PDF]]|access-date=24 March 2013}}</ref> which described how the Dimensionist tendency has led to:
# Literature leaving the line and entering the plane.
# Painting leaving the plane and entering space.
# Sculpture stepping out of closed, immobile forms.
# The artistic conquest of four-dimensional space, which to date has been completely art-free.

The manifesto was signed by many prominent modern artists worldwide. [[Hans Arp]], [[Francis Picabia]], [[Wassily Kandinsky|Kandinsky]], [[Robert Delaunay]] and Marcel Duchamp amongst others added their names in Paris, then a short while later it was endorsed by artists abroad including [[László Moholy-Nagy]], [[Joan Miró]], [[David Kakabadze]], [[Alexander Calder]], and [[Ben Nicholson]].<ref name="dimensionalist" />

== ''Crucifixion (Corpus Hypercubus)'' ==

In 1953, the [[surrealist]] [[Salvador Dalí]] proclaimed his intention to paint "an explosive, nuclear and hypercubic" crucifixion scene.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Dalí |first1=Salvador |author-link1=Salvador Dalí|last2=Gómez de la Serna|first2=Ramón  |title=Dali |location=Secaucus, NJ |publisher=Wellfleet Press |orig-year=1988 |year=2001  |page=41 |isbn=1-55521-342-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.spanisharts.com/history/del_impres_s.XX/arte_sXX/vanguardias1/i_surrealismo_dali.html |title=Salvador Dalí (1904–1989) |publisher=SpanishArts |year=2013 |access-date=24 March 2013 |archive-date=16 May 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120516012456/http://spanisharts.com/history/del_impres_s.XX/arte_sXX/vanguardias1/i_surrealismo_dali.html |url-status=usurped }}</ref> He said that, "This picture will be the great metaphysical work of my summer".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dali-gallery.com/html/analyses/1954_02a.htm |title=Crucifixion ('Corpus Hypercubus'), 1954 |publisher=Dalí gallery website |access-date=25 March 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130613025908/http://www.dali-gallery.com/html/analyses/1954_02a.htm |archive-date=13 June 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Completed the next year, ''[[Crucifixion (Corpus Hypercubus)]]'' depicts Jesus Christ upon the net of a hypercube, also known as a [[tesseract]]. The unfolding of a tesseract into eight cubes is analogous to unfolding the sides of a cube into six squares. The [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]] describes the painting as a "new interpretation of an oft-depicted subject. ..[showing] Christ's spiritual triumph over corporeal harm."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.metmuseum.org/collections/search-the-collections/210009107 |title= ''Crucifixion (Corpus Hypercubus)'' |publisher=The Metropolitan Museum of Art |access-date=24 March 2013}}</ref>

== Abstract art ==
The concept of the fourth-dimension, and other geometries, influenced artists of the early twentieth century. The definition of the fourth-dimension differed from artist to artist: before [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]], artists would associate the term with an extra spatial dimension; after Einstein's theory of relativity was [[Eddington experiment|vindicated]] in 1919, the fourth-dimension became associated with ''time'' rather than space.{{sfnp|Henderson|2013}}

Between 1913 to 1915, [[Piet Mondrian]] produced paintings employing the ''spatial'' interpretation of this principle in his ''Pier and Ocean'' series. By 1917 he had developed his theory of [[Neo-plasticism]] which excluded this principle in favour of colour planes and orthogonal lines on a flat surface.{{sfnp|Kruger|2007}} His close collaborator, [[Theo van Doesburg]] showed an early interest in the spatial fourth-dimension, later developing his interest to include the temporal dimension in his works. Mondrian rejected both interpretations in favour of stasis ,{{sfnp|Baljeu|1968}} and this difference of views played a major role in his departure from [[De Stijl]] in 1924.{{sfnp|Blotkamp|1994|pages=147-148}} Van Doesburg went on to develop [[Elementarism]], incorporating the dynamic concept of movement and expansion.{{sfnp|Blotkamp|1982|pages=29-32}}{{sfnp|Ubink|1918}}

== Other forms of art ==
{{Main|Fourth dimension in literature}}

The fourth dimension has been the subject of numerous fictional stories.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.strangehorizons.com/2002/20020916/fourth_dimension.shtml |title=Spirits, Art, and the Fourth Dimension |first1=Bryan |last1=Clair |date=16 September 2002 |publisher=[[Strange Horizons]] |access-date=25 March 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120107143452/http://www.strangehorizons.com/2002/20020916/fourth_dimension.shtml |archive-date=7 January 2012 }}</ref>
